en: Śrīḥ!
A Garland of Verses on the Meaning of the Brahma Sūtras.
Prosperity!

Having meditated upon the lotus feet of the Lord of Sages known as Śrī Ṅga-Śaṭhakopa, and having bowed to the Lord of Sages Śrī Vīrarāghavendra and Śaṭharipu, Rājagopāla—who was looked upon with favor by those two preeminent lords of sages—composes this garland of verses for awakening the meaning of the Brahma-sūtras.
The first quarter of the first chapter.
Having understood through reflection that the fruit of ritual action is very small, one who desires liberation and seeks the infinity of results must undertake the inquiry into Brahman.
The Śruti has declared that Brahman is that from which the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of this world proceed—that which is omniscient and whose will is ever-true.
Since the Supreme Self, the source of the world, is to be known through scripture alone and cannot be inferred, scripture is meaningful in this context.

However, the status of the Veda as having the scripture alone as its cause is well-established, because it is connected to that [scripture] both by virtue of being for the sake of human ends and by virtue of being the means of cognition.
The Pradhāna is not denoted here by words such as "with the gods" and so forth; because of the presence of the act of seeing (īkṣati), the term "Being" (sat) refers to Brahman.
"If it be argued that this act of seeing belongs to the secondary [Self] and that the 'Being' is inferential, we say no; for the word 'Being' is qualified by the word 'Self'."
Since liberation is taught here for one who worships the true object, that [liberation] would be the attainment of the Pradhāna; if this were so, liberation would not partake of bliss.

That which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) is not to be meditated upon because it is to be abandoned—this is not stated; rather, since it is described precisely as an object of meditation, the bliss of Brahman is called "Sat."
For it is held that knowledge of the effect arises from knowledge of the cause; moreover, because this would contradict their own thesis, the Pradhāna cannot be the cause.
And because of the statement regarding dissolution into the cause, the primary cause of the dissolution of one's own self is indeed Brahman; thus, the Pradhāna is not denoted by the word "Sat."
Just as the activity of sentences is observed to consist in the expression of a cause, so too, because of that similarity, the meaning of the word "Being" (sat) is the Supreme Person.
Because it is heard in scripture that "this [world] belongs to the Self alone," the Pradhāna cannot be the cause here; rather, Brahman alone is indeed its cause.

For the Supreme Self is indeed denoted by the word "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), because it possesses a hundredfold bliss as stated in the scriptural passage beginning with "those who are a hundred."

If it is argued that the suffix *mayaṭ* does not signify "consisting of" (as in *brahmamaya*) because it denotes a modification (*vikāra*), we say no; for this *mayaṭ* signifies abundance (*prācurya*), since it follows [the word] *para*.

Because of the scriptural statement, "He indeed causes bliss," and because of the designation of [the Self] as the cause of the bliss of the Self, that which consists of the bliss of Brahman must be the Self.
That which is declared in the words of the Mantras as truth, knowledge, and infinite, is likewise celebrated by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) as the Supreme.
This person of limited intellect is declared by the words of the mantra to be other than Brahman, specifically because the resolve "May I become many" is otherwise untenable.

Because this [Self] is proclaimed as distinct from the living self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), it is the Brahman itself that is taught here in the passage beginning with "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

Since the creation of the world proceeds from His will alone, without any contact with insentient matter, and because of the scriptural statement "May I be many," the individual soul (jīva) is certainly not its cause.

In this great bliss, the attainment of bliss by the individual soul (jīva) is described; for the scripture states, "Having attained it, he becomes blissful. Therefore, [the Self] consists of the bliss of Brahman.
He who is within the sun, the eye, is that Supreme Self, golden-hued, because he has risen above all sins and is devoid of those qualities [such as hunger and thirst] associated with them.
Because of the teaching of His distinction from the sun—namely, "He who stands in the sun"—the Supreme Person is other than the individual soul (jīva).
"Space is the Supreme Self"—this is stated here because of its characteristic marks, specifically due to the qualifying attributes of being the ultimate resort and the cause of creation and so forth.

For this very reason, on account of the previously mentioned indicative mark, the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be Brahman; for the designation [of it as Brahman] is based on its being the life-force of all living beings, just like a well-known usage.
The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is indicated by the words "the light beyond heaven," because He is proclaimed to be the feet of the entire multitude of beings.

If it is argued that this is not so because the term "Gāyatrī" is used in the opening section to denote the non-conscious [element], we say no; for that is likewise intended as a meditation on the Supreme Self through the metaphor of similarity.
On account of the logical consistency of the mention of the elements, the earth, the body, and so forth as its feet, it is understood that what is designated by the word "Gāyatrī" is indeed Brahman.

In one instance, the word "divi" is used with the locative case, while in another, "divaḥ" is used with the ablative; because of this difference in expression, the [particle] "paraḥ" (beyond) is not [applied] in both cases, as there is no contradiction.
The Self of Indra, indicated by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa," is to be meditated upon as Brahman, because of the observation of the concluding statement regarding bliss, nectar, sound, and so forth.

If it is argued that Indra himself is meant because of the injunction, "Meditate on me as the Self, the speaker, who is Indra," we say no; for here [the Self] is connected with the quality of Brahman-bliss.

The injunction "Know me as the Brahman whose body is the universe" arises from knowledge of the scriptures; and here, as in the case of Vāmadeva and others, the wielder of the thunderbolt says, "Worship me."

If it is argued that the term "Brahman" does not apply here because of the mention of Indra, Jīva, and Prāṇa, we say no; for elsewhere there is a threefold meditation, just as it is described here through the narrative.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the Garland of Verses on the Meaning of the Brahma Sūtras.
Now begins the second quarter of the first chapter.
By the teaching that "all this indeed [is Brahman]," it is declared that the Supreme Self alone, who is the Self of all, consists of mind.

Since the qualities about to be described are possible only in the Supreme, it is appropriate that the state of being meditated upon as "born from, dissolved in, and breathing in Him" (tajjalān) applies to the Supreme Self alone.

The living being (jīva) here is not mind-made (manomaya), because the capacity for creation and so forth is impossible [for it], and because it is proclaimed that everywhere, multiplicity arises through mere volition (saṅkalpa).

Because of the statement regarding the agency of the action—"I am to be attained after departing"—the object to be attained here is indeed Brahman, which is the cause for both the one who attains and the meditator.

The [passage beginning with] "This which is the self" and so forth indicates those two [the self and the mind-made] by means of the genitive and the nominative cases respectively; between the meanings of those two nominatives, the one ending in the nominative is the mind-made (manomaya).

And by the very memory of "I" and so forth in everyone, the Supreme Lord—who is distinct from the individual soul—is established within the heart as the giver of that memory and the bestower of knowledge.
If it is argued that He is not the Lord because of the designation of His being small and occupying a limited space, we say no; for He is to be perceived as such, and thus, like space, He is great.
If it is argued that the Supreme Self, like the individual soul (jīva), would experience suffering and so forth while residing in the heart, we say no; for karma is indeed the cause of this.
The Self indicated there is indeed the Destroyer; the certainty is that He is the Supreme Self. For the world exists as food for the Brahmin and the Kshatriya, with death as its seasoning.

Because of the introductory context beginning with "the Great, the All-pervading," He is indeed the Supreme; and by the statement "the Eater of the moving and the unmoving," He is the destroyer of the world.

The two who have entered the cave are indeed the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (para), and not the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul; for it is said that "they" alone enter the cave-dwelling.
In these very two contexts, because they are specifically described as the object of meditation and the meditator, it is the Brahman and the individual soul that are hidden in the cave.
The person dwelling within the eye is none other than the reflection of the individual soul (jīva), because of the logical consistency of such qualities as immortality and fearlessness.

And because of the scriptural statement "He who [is] the eyes," because of the designation of His abiding therein, and because of such qualities as eternal hunger and immortality, the Supreme Person is distinct [from the individual soul].
Since the term "Ka" is used here to denote the blissful state for the purpose of meditation, and because of its mention and stability within this context, the Supreme Person resides within the heart.

Therefore, because of the mention of "the Brahman is Ka, the Brahman is Kha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5), and since that [Brahman] has space as its support, it is indeed the Supreme Person who is meant by "space."

For the path beginning with light (arcis) and so forth, which is declared for those who have heard the Upaniṣads, is said here to belong to the worshiper as well; therefore, he too is the Supreme Person.

Because it necessarily functions within the imperceptible, the individual soul (jīva) and so forth cannot be the object of sight here; for [if they were], the previously mentioned impossibilities, such as being a controller and possessing immortality, would follow.

The Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) mentioned in the sections concerning the deities, the worlds, and so forth, is the Supreme Being, because he is praised as possessing the attribute of being the controller of all that is to be known.

The Pradhāna and the individual soul (jīva) are certainly not what are meant here by the term "inner controller" (antaryāmin), because attributes impossible for them are predicated here [of that inner controller].
"He who is in both, in the inner controller, in consciousness, and in the self"—thus they study him as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), just like the eye and other organs.

The Imperishable (akṣara), characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so forth, is the Supreme Person; yet, because of the mention of attributes such as omniscience, He is higher than that which is beyond the Imperishable.

The Imperishable (akṣara) must be none other than the one from whom, through the knowledge of oneself, comes the knowledge of all; for it is heard in scripture as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), being described as higher than the Imperishable and as that which is beyond the individual soul.
In the two syllables "Agni is the head, the moon and sun are the eyes," the Supreme Lord is praised as the embodiment of all the gods and other limbs.
Vaiśvānara is the supreme Brahman, distinct from the insentient and so forth, because the general term "Brahman" and others are qualified by specific attributes.

The form described in the Brāhmaṇa as "Agni is the head," which is heard in the Śruti and recorded in the Smṛti, is Vaiśvānara; by recollecting that supreme Brāhma-form here [in this practice], [one attains the goal].

If it is argued that the Brāhmaṇa does not [teach this] because of the scriptural statement regarding the internal fire as the locus of the oblation, that is not so; for that [instruction] is for the sake of the meditation of a person whose body is the digestive fire.
Because he has the three worlds as his body and is celebrated as the Puruṣa, Vaiśvānara is neither the deity Agni nor the third element (fire).
Jaimini declared that there is no contradiction with the Brāhmaṇa passage, because the word "Agni" also denotes Vaiśvānara through its etymological derivation (yoga) and its power to signify.
However, the opinion of the sage Āśmarathya is that here [in this context], the soul is limited by measures such as "having the sky as its head," because of its manifestation within the worshipper.
Bādari declared that the conceptualization of the heavenly world and so forth as the head and other limbs is intended for the purpose of teaching meditation in that very manner.

Jaimini, however, maintains that because the nature of the Agnihotra is fully realized through the oblation to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti), there is the conceptualization [of the body] as the altar and so forth; for indeed, the Śruti declares this.

Having meditated upon the limbs beginning with "the radiant head" (dyumūrdhā) within the body of the worshipper, he then contemplated Vaiśvānara here for the purpose of offering oblations and worship.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Brahmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.

They know that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Brahman, as well as its support within the channels (nāḍī); for here [in the scripture] there are such statements as "by its own word" and "this is the bridge of immortality."
When, O seer, one beholds the golden-hued [Self] during this stage of progression, he attains supreme equanimity; thus it is heard from the Śruti regarding the support of heaven and earth.
And like the Pradhāna, the individual soul (jīva) also cannot be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; for it is established that there is an absence of words denoting it [in this context].
Since the scripture states, "When he sees the other as the Lord," and because they are designated here as distinct from one another, the individual soul (jīva) is not the sustainer of all.

Moreover, from the context of the preceding Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "He went forth," it must be determined that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Brahman, and not anything else here.

Abiding in one and the same body, one [the individual soul] remains without eating the fruit while being self-ruling; whereas the other, the Supreme Person, eats while making the living being live—thus, in that regard, the Supreme Person is the non-enjoyer.
Because of the specific instruction given by the teacher Sanatkumāra to Nārada regarding that which is superior to the individual soul (jīva), the "Bhūman" here is the Supreme Person.
It is established in its own majesty here, according to the scriptural statement "Bhūman"; it is supreme because it has no other support and because it possesses such qualities.

The supreme Brahman, however, is the Imperishable (akṣara), because it sustains the unmanifest here, and because it is perceived as that which pervades everything as the warp and is woven across it as the woof.
Because it is declared that "in the governance and the maintenance of the Imperishable," that maintenance arises from governance; therefore, the ignorant soul (jīva) is not the Imperishable.
Because the Śruti declares, "The unseen Seer," and because it negates the state of being an object, the Imperishable (akṣara) is indeed said to be the Supreme Self, the cause of the universe.
Because of the praise of agelessness and other qualities in the passage "He who beholds the Puruṣa," this Puruṣa is the Supreme Person, distinct from the four-faced Brahmā.

The Supreme Self is indeed called "dahara" (the small) because it is described as being "within this small [space]"; this is understood from the subsequent passages which establish its connection with specific attributes.

In that context, the "small" (dahara) is the Supreme, on account of the words "going" (gati) and "world of Brahman" (brāhmaloka), and because of the indicative marks of another scriptural passage stating, "He attains the world of Brahman."
Because it serves to maintain the non-confusion of the worlds and to sustain their majesty here, and because that Supreme One is heard of within it, the "small" space is indeed the Supreme.

For that well-known reality which is accompanied by the vital breaths and so forth is indeed powerful; therefore, the Supreme Person is more difficult to burn away than even the well-known elemental ether and the like.

If it be argued that because the individual soul (jīva) is referred to here by the term "serenity" (saṃprasāda), and because the word "he" (saḥ) occurs in the subsequent portion of the passage, [the Self under discussion] is the jīva—no, for the jīva is not possible [in this context].

If it be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is meant here because of the scriptural passage beginning with "the Self which is free from sin," we reply: in that case, since the text describes the manifestation of its true nature, the jīva cannot be the one who is "small" (dahara).

The mention of the Brāhmaṇas therein is for the purpose of declaring their greatness; [it refers] to the state of serene confidence (saṃprasāda) and so forth, by means of the attainment of one's true nature and other such factors, leading to liberation.

If it is argued that Brahman is not [the cause] because of scriptural statements regarding its smallness and its existence in a limited place, this has already been answered previously by the statement: "Because it is to be perceived as such."

Based on the scriptural statement beginning with "the supreme equality" and because of the imitation of that equality, the individual soul (jīva) is the imitator, while the Supreme Person within the small space (dahara) is the object of imitation.

"Having resorted to this knowledge, they have attained a state of similarity with me"—this traditional teaching (smṛti) shows that the individual soul (jīva) is an imitator; thus, [the claim that it is] the cause [of the world] is not valid.
The person the size of a thumb mentioned in the Kaṭhavallī is indeed the Supreme Person, precisely because of the scriptural statement regarding His lordship over the past, the future, and so forth.
Because the Supreme Self is the object of worship for human beings, its measurement as the size of a thumb occurs with reference to the heart.
The meditation of the gods is possible because of their desire and because it is feasible; the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers it to be exactly so.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding the gods possessing bodies in relation to their actions, it is not so; for we observe in the case of Saubhari and others the attainment of various forms.

If it were argued that "the Veda would possess non-eternal meaning upon the destruction of the bodies of the gods and others," this is incorrect, because of the Śruti and Smṛti which state that [the world] was created from the Word (Śabda).

According to the Vedic scripture, "The Creator [fashioned] the sun and moon as before," let it be that the Creator, having recollected the established state, creates; thus, there is eternal continuity.
Furthermore, because the names and forms remain the same, the Brahman creates again; thus, there is no contradiction even regarding dissolution, as is understood from both Śruti and Smṛti.

Furthermore, because they have already attained the status of Vasus and because they themselves are objects of worship, Jaimini maintains that the Vasus have no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations.
"The gods meditate upon light"—in such Vedic reflections, this [meditation] is understood as being for those who possess the qualification [for it], while there is no qualification for others.
Bādarāyaṇa has declared that for those who desire to attain the status of a Vasu in another birth, there may be the worship of another deity while remaining independent.

Because he ran toward his guru at that very moment upon hearing the disrespectful words of the swan, the latter addressed him as "Śūdra" out of grief; however, this did not mean he was actually a Śūdra.
However, since Jānaśruti is seen to have given many gifts in that very context, his status as a Kṣatriya is understood; therefore, a Śūdra has no entitlement [to this knowledge].
Furthermore, from the subsequent mention of Vidyā, it is understood that [Abhipratārin] was a Kṣatriya; for they caused Caitraratha to perform sacrifices on behalf of Abhipratārin.

Because of the investigation of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) in the section concerning the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmī vidyā*), and because of the statement regarding the absence of such rites, the Śūdra does not possess the qualification [for that knowledge].
Since it is certain that Jābāli’s attendant was not a Śūdra, and because he engaged in receiving instruction, a Śūdra does not possess the qualification [for Vedic study].

It is certain that a Śūdra has no entitlement even to meditative worship, because of the prohibitions against hearing the sacred tradition, studying it, and performing sacrifices and other such rites.
Furthermore, from such Smṛti texts as "One should not teach him the Dharma," it is understood that a Śūdra has no qualification for meditative worship (upāsana).

(Conclusion of the section on the measured [prāṇa]: Because of the fear arising from the Brahman designated by the term "the vital breath measured by a thumb," all the gods remain ever-watchful; such is the supreme [Brahman] according to the Śruti.
"Indeed, the Supreme is thumb-sized, because it is seen right here; for it is heard in scripture that 'by its light all this shines.
Since it is heard in this scripture that 'by its light all this shines,' and because the most excellent light is perceived, He is the Supreme Person."
The Supreme Lord is the space that carries away name-and-form (nāmarūpa), because He is proclaimed as being distinct from the three states of bound, liberated, and both.

In deep sleep, he is described as being completely embraced by the Wise One; likewise, at the time of departure, [he departs] separately from that. Therefore, the Supreme Person is other than the individual soul (jīva).
Furthermore, by designations such as "the sovereign lord of all" and so forth, it is firmly established that this Supreme Self is the Knower and is distinct from the individual soul (jīva).
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Brahmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the first chapter.
If it is argued that some say even the Pradhāna is the cause, [we reply] no; for the body arranged in the form of a chariot is what is called the Unmanifest (avyakta).
For that very same unmanifest [state], residing in the body, is indeed fit for active engagement; therefore, it is not the Pradhāna that is denoted here by the word "unmanifest."

The characterization of [the body] as a chariot and so forth, by virtue of its dependence on the Supreme Self, would be purposeful; however, that which is "unmanifest" (avyakta) according to the Tantras has no such purpose here.
The Pradhāna is not mentioned here as an object of knowledge, because it is their [the Sāṃkhyas'] view that liberation arises from the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower.

If it is argued that the Śruti declares "that which is to be known is soundless and touchless," we say no; for, by virtue of the context, it is indeed the Supreme Self (paramātman) that is being described.
Here, one asks about the worship, the object of worship, and the meditator; among these three instructions, that [which concerns the meditator] is not said to be the primary one here.
Just as the principle of Mahat is not grasped because it is qualified by the word "Self," so too the Pradhāna is not grasped because the Self is superior to it.

Just as the cup [of Soma] is designated as "this is its head," so too [the goat] is not the one spoken of by the opponent, because there is no distinction in the case of the goat; for that [goat] is indeed the one referred to.
That [text], however, is a Brāhmaṇa passage; the Taittirīyas read it there as "He who is subtler than the subtle," referring to the heart which is presided over by light.

Just as the state of being honey and the status of being an effect belong to the sun by virtue of its oneness with that which abides [as honey], so too would it be for the Unborn (Ajā) on account of scriptural statements regarding creation and so forth.

Nor is the Sāṃkhya system applicable here, for even in the case of the grasping of the twilight [periods], there are five times five persons; thus, due to both diversity and excess, the process described by the Sāṃkhyas does not hold.
The five people (pañcajana) are determined to be the vital breaths and so forth, for the concluding portion of the sentence is seen to be "the breath of breath" and so on.
Even for those reciters of the Veda who do not have the reading beginning with "of some [the food]," let the sense organs indeed be understood by the word "lights" (jyotiṣām).

The causality of the Omniscient One was previously declared in relation to space and so forth; furthermore, in the passage "In the beginning this was non-existent," his very nature is stated to be the cause.
In passages such as "In the beginning, this was non-existent," it is the Veda itself that is the cause here as well, for it draws forth and declares the omniscient, universal cause.
Or rather, it is heard that this world is the "action" (karman) of Him; for in the Śruti, the individual soul (jīva) is not said to be subject to merit and so forth.

If it is argued that Brahman cannot be the cause because of the mention of the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa), it has been explained [in the commentary] that this is for the sake of establishing the threefold meditation.

Jaimini maintains that this reference to the individual soul (jīva) is for the purpose of establishing its difference from the [Supreme] Soul; thus he says, based on both the question and the explanation, and so too the Śruti.
From the sequence of statements in the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa, it follows that the Self described as "to be seen" is the Supreme Self (paramātman), not the one belonging to the Tantras.
In order to establish the proposition, the mention of the term "Brahman" by means of words that denote the individual soul (jīva) is the mark [of Brahman]; this is the opinion of the sage Āśmarathya.

The statement regarding another person being made by means of the living self (jīva) belongs indeed to one who is about to depart; this is the view of Auḍulomi, who fell away from the [doctrine of] identity with Brahman.
And because the Brahman abides within the self, its designation by means of terms denoting the individual soul is appropriate; such is the opinion of the sage Kāśakṛtsna.

And that [self] is the substratum for the grasping [of the aggregates], likewise for the sake of establishing the proposition, because there is no sublation of the examples such as gold, bracelets, and so forth.
It is certain that the resolve "May I be many," as expressed by the Śruti, is itself the cause of this world, serving as both its material and efficient cause.
The material cause and the efficient cause of the world must be Brahman, because of such declarations as "Brahman is the forest" and "Brahman is the tree."
Because it brings about its own multiplicity, it is indeed both the agent and the object; therefore, Brahman is said to be both the efficient cause and the material cause.
The subtle, insentient, conscious entity [is distinct] from the body; the manifold transformation of the Brahman within the body does not constitute its destruction.
It is certain that, according to such scriptural passages as "That which is the source of all beings," Brahman is proclaimed to be the material cause of the entire universe.
By this reasoning up to this point, it is certain that all the Vedāntas, which propound a cause, are revealers of the Supreme Brahman.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Brahmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*.

Thus ends the first chapter of the *Brāhmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*, the work of the venerable Śrī Vāṇśaṭhakopa Vedāntadeśika Yatīndra Mahādeśika, who is adorned by forty-four consecrations as pontiff at the divine seat of the venerable Ahobilamaṭha, and who is enriched by the array of titles beginning with "Śrīmadvedamārga."
Now begins the first quarter of the second chapter.
If the Pradhāna were not the cause, the Smṛti of Kapila would be abandoned; thus, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not out of joy regarding what is not the truth of Brahman.
But for other sages, since no causality toward the world is perceived in their primary principle, Brahman alone must be the cause of everything without exception.
The Smṛti of the wise which declares that "the heart is merely a sign" has already been refuted by the force of Śruti, according to the very reasoning previously stated.
Causality is not established by way of being distinct from the world; rather, the nature of Brahman as both "being" (sat) and "that which is evolved" (tyat) is established through scripture.
Out of the desire to speak with pride, the Earth said to him, "The deities have vanished," even though their entry had already been proclaimed.
Just as the production of honey and other such things from bees and so forth is entirely logical, so too is the production of the world from the Brahman, though it is of a different nature.

If it is argued that this would result in the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (asatkāryavāda), we say no; for here, the restriction of similarity between the two is merely being negated.

Since the world exists during both the period of dissolution and the time of creation, the Supreme Self is not distinct from it; therefore, the defects of the world would belong to Brahman, and thus His statement would be inconsistent.
Just as the qualities (guṇas) are established in relation to the self and the body, so too is the world established in relation to Brahman; this is indeed consistent.
O sinless one, since there are many defects in your own position, you should abandon your own view and accept the faultless doctrine that Brahman is the cause.
Because fallacious reasoning is unstable, the Pradhāna is not the cause, since it was postulated by you through mere argumentation without being presided over by Brahmā.
If it is argued that the Pradhāna is established through the force of reasoning, then you would not be released from the refutation by even more powerful reasoning.
The learned have rejected those who do not accept the Vedas, just as they have rejected the Sāṅkhya position, because their views are rooted in fallacious reasoning and are mutually contradictory.

If it is argued that since Brahman constitutes the entire body, its status as an enjoyer would be like that of the individual soul (jīva), and therefore there is no distinction [between them], then even if [Brahman] were omnipresent, it could not be an enjoyer.
The non-difference of the world from Brahman, its cause, arises here from such passages as "beginning with speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4), just as a jar is non-different from a lump of clay.
Because gold is perceived within its effects such as earrings and the like, it is the opinion of those who know the Vedas that the effect is non-different from the cause.
But because another effect exists in a subtle state within its own cause, the effect is non-different from the cause; for indeed, the jar exists subtly in the clay.

If it be argued that [the Self] does not exist because it is designated as "not this, not this," we say no, for it exists due to its subtlety. This designation [of non-existence] arises from the remainder of the sentence, from reasoning, and likewise from other scriptural passages.
Just as in the world threads, through a particular kind of interconnection that touches upon other names and forms, are designated as "cloth," so too [is the case with the elements].
Just as the vital breath (prāṇa) and the other winds do not become something other than air despite the difference in their locations, so too the world is not other than Brahman, its own cause.

Furthermore, it is objected that because of the designation of "livingness" (jīvatva) and due to defects such as performing what is beneficial or harmful, the status of Brahman as the cause cannot be established.

Because this very [Self] is taught in the scripture as the "Lord of the lords of causes" through differentiation, the Brāhmaṇa is superior; therefore, the soul (jīva) is not [the subject] here, nor is the intellect (duḥstha).
Just as it is not possible for stones and the like to attain the state of Brahman, so too it is not appropriate for the individual soul, which is filled with a flood of sins.
For even one who is capable is seen to require assistance; therefore, the Brahman is without a second, just as curds do not exist apart from milk.
Just as the gods and others create various things within their respective worlds, so too does Brahmā extend the entire universe through his own volition.
How could the entire Brahman come to be through the resolve "May I be many"? For if it were possessed of parts, there would be a contradiction with those statements that declare it to be partless.
Because it is known through the mere word, the Śruti would speak of Brahman; since everything has that as its cause, the Śruti is entirely consistent.

Just as the properties of non-intelligence do not attach to the individual soul (jīvātman), so too [non-existence] does not attach to the Supreme; and just as heat and other such powers do not reside in water and the like, so they do not reside in the Supreme.
How could a partless primordial matter (pradhāna) possess causality? Since that fault exists in your own position, let the Unmanifest alone be the cause.
The supreme deity, endowed with all diverse powers and accompanied by the syllable *hrūm*, is to be worshipped as established by the Vedas; thus she is called the cause of the universe.

If it is argued that [the argument] is not a valid reason because [the Supreme Self] is devoid of sense organs, that has already been answered; for it is stated in the scripture, "Neither an effect nor an instrument belongs to that Supreme Self."
It is objected that, because the purpose of creation pervades [all things], the Supreme Self—being devoid of such a purpose and being perfectly complete—could not be the creator.
Just as one who possesses a complete set of balls and other playthings engages in sport, so too the purpose of the creation of the perfect Brahman is mere divine play (līlā).
There is neither partiality nor cruelty in the Lord who creates beings such as the low-born and others; for the Śruti demonstrates this by showing that He acts in accordance with their past karma.

If it is argued that because there is no division due to the absence of a living soul (jīva), action does not exist at that time, [we reply]: the lack of division is also logically established by the scriptural statement that the living soul is beginningless.

Whatever refutation applies to the theories of primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth as causes, that does not apply to the Brahman as cause, because all phenomena are established within it.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Garland of Verses on the Meaning of the Brahma Sūtras.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter.

Furthermore, because creation and so forth are otherwise inexplicable, inference cannot be the cause [of the world], since this [universe] proceeds toward its creation only when presided over by Brahman.
Just as the production of curd from milk and of mango-juice from water occurs, so too would it be here; it is not otherwise, for even in that case there is the conjunction with the wise.

If its activity were independent [of causes], there would indeed be creation at all times; and because of the absence of dissolution and so forth, the established order of things could not be established.
If it is argued that grass and the like are the very nature of milk, then that same grass consumed by a bull would not become milk.
Just as a lame man and a blind man employ a magnet, so too do Pradhāna and Puruṣa; thus there would never be a lack of agency.

At the time of dissolution, there would be an equilibrium of the qualities, such as sattva and the rest; however, because it is impossible for a single quality to function as the predominant factor (aṅgin), [the existence of such a state] is untenable.
And here, in the inference of the Pradhāna, if it were otherwise, then because of the absence of the power of being a knower, the impossibility of [its] arrangement and so forth would follow.

Even though the primary cause (pradhāna) is the means of accomplishment here, there would be the opposite result due to the absence of a fruit; moreover, enjoyment and liberation would not occur because the primary cause would remain eternally present.

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya system is inconsistent due to internal contradictions, because it attempts to establish the capacity for being a seer and so forth in that which is both untainted and changeless.
"It is inconsistent that a dyad arises from two atoms; and it is also inconsistent that from dyads there arise the large and the long."
Furthermore, since action itself is only occasional, it cannot be the cause of the circular and the living being; thus, the categories of "large" and "long" are not established.

Because of the admission of inherence (samavāya) and because that [inherence] also exists as non-distinct [from its substrates], there is a dependence on further causes; thus, due to infinite regress, that [system] is indeed inconsistent.
Furthermore, if the relation were eternal, the eternity of the world of related entities would necessarily follow; thus, that [position] is indeed inconsistent.
The atom is impermanent because it is necessarily possessed of form and the like; for it is observed that jars and other such things, being possessed of form, are impermanent.

But for those whose qualities are restricted to their effects, there is no cause other than the quality residing in the cause; this is because, if that [cause] were present, the effect would exist, and if it were absent, there would be a fault [of non-existence].
Since this doctrine of Kaṇāda is not accepted in its entirety by the wise, seekers of liberation should always maintain a disregard for it.
By asserting the momentariness of all things, neither the composite whole rooted in atoms nor the composite body and so forth commenced by the primary elements (bhūtas) could exist for us.

If it is argued that the world arises from ignorance and the rest because they function as mutual causes, we say no; for even so, this [ignorance] lacks causality when it exists as a composite aggregate.
Since the cause has perished at the time of the production of the effect, it cannot indeed be the cause; for if non-existence were the cause, the entire world would exist at all times.
If the effect were to exist when the cause is absent, the proposition would be contradicted; for there are four types of causes, otherwise there would be simultaneity.
If it is argued that gross and subtle destructions are without residue (niranvaya), we say no; because another state exists, destruction is not without residue.
For you who assert that what has arisen is insubstantial and that even its emergence is from the insubstantial, the entire world must surely be insubstantial.
Because the perception of the world is uniform, even space cannot be non-existent; for the perception that "a hawk is flying here" is not sublated.
Furthermore, the recognition "this is that very same jar" arises; therefore, the momentariness of effects such as jars is not established.
When objects have perished, their quality is not observed to transfer to another thing; therefore, momentariness is not tenable.
In that system where a result arises even for one who exerts effort toward its destruction, liberation and the like would likewise arise for those who make no effort at all.
The assertion that things other than cognition do not exist is not established, because all objects are apprehended through valid means of knowledge.
Just as in dreams and similar states, the falsity of waking cognition is not tenable; rather, its truth follows precisely from its dissimilarity to [states] characterized by the presence of defects.
Furthermore, the existence of a cognition devoid of an object is not found at all, because a cognition that is separated from both action and agent is unperceived.

Furthermore, the doctrine of universal emptiness cannot be established according to your own view, because it is entirely untenable and contradicts the means of valid cognition and other such criteria.

The simultaneous assertion that [an entity] both exists and does not exist in one and the same thing is rejected because it is impossible, as is the doctrine of being both different and non-different.
If the self were of the same size as that body, it would be incomplete; for when one who has resided in the body of an elephant then enters the body of an ant.
Even when there is a connection with different states, no contradiction is established; for if the self were subject to modification, it would be equal to a jar or other such objects.
Since both the liberated self and the size of that liberated self are eternal, the living being (jīva) does not possess the same dimensions as the body.

The doctrine of Paśupati must also be abandoned by those seeking liberation, because it contradicts the conduct prescribed by the Vedas and because it involves distinctions such as [the division between] the material cause and so forth.
The creation of the world by a bodiless Lord is not established, because, like a potter, his presiding over [the material cause] is untenable due to contradiction.

If it is argued that the Unborn (the Lord) presides over [the world] just as the individual soul (jīva) accepts [its own] appropriation, then it follows that action, experience, and so forth would belong to the Lord just as they do to the individual soul.

If that [creator] were also unseen, then [the world] would follow as being created by him and so forth; furthermore, there would be a loss of his omniscience. Therefore, that [position] is not tenable.

Furthermore, the doctrine of the soul's origination and so forth is observed in the Pañcarātra; however, because it contradicts the scriptural teaching that such origination is impossible, it is inconsistent.
The mind, as an instrument, does not arise from the agent or the individual soul (jīva); for it is taught that the birth of the mind is from Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is the individual soul.
However, because Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others are determined to be the Supreme Self, their status as incarnations who identify with individual souls does not invalidate their authority.
Since even in this Pañcarātra Tantra the production of the individual soul (jīva) is denied, this Tantra is correct and should be accepted by one desiring liberation.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Brahmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*.
Now begins the third quarter of the second chapter.
He raises the objection that there is no origination of the all-pervading ether because there is no statement regarding its origination, and because it is eternal like the self (ātman).
Because the Veda declares that "from the Self, space was produced," it is certain that the origination of that space exists.

The scriptural mention of the origin of space may be figurative, because its actual production is impossible, and because it is associated with fire as the first element, and also because of the scriptural mention of its immortality.

In this case as well, the single word "saṃbhūta" possesses both a secondary (gauṇa) and a primary (mukhya) sense; and here too, the word "brāhma," which is applied by extension (anuṣakta), retains its primary sense.
Because there is no abandonment of the initial proposition and because space is an effect, it is understood that the creation of space is intended even in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
From such scriptural statements as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and so forth, because the ether is the body of Brahman, the ether is an effect of Brahman.
By the Śruti statement "All this has that as its self," the state of being a modification of everything is established; thus, the origination of all things occurs from Brahman, just as in the world.
Likewise, since it is stated that "from space, air [arises]" and "from the word, the Veda," it is certain that the nature of the Veda as an effect has been explained.
From every cause, the arising of another [entity] is nowhere possible; for such a thesis is untenable, and everything else is born from that which is other than itself.
Fire is produced from air; therefore, it does not have Brahman as its material cause. Based on the Vedic scripture "From air, fire," one might suspect that fire has air as its material cause.
And since water is created by fire, one might raise the doubt as to how it can serve the purpose of Brahman, given the Vedic scripture stating, "Water [is produced] from fire."
The earth was born from the waters; therefore, it is not indeed born of Brahman. How can it be specifically said that she is fit for the work of Brahman?
The statement "they created food" refers to the creation of the earth; for from words signifying the domain of the elements, it is understood that "food" means the earth.
From the volition "May I become many," and by means of the subtle body (liṅga) created from his own nature, the Lord, possessing a progressively earlier body, creates each subsequent one.
In this context, because the sequence of immediate succession is reversed through tradition, the creation of those respective bodies and so forth is established as belonging to Brahmā.

If it is argued that the sense organs arise in sequence between the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the gross elements (bhūtas) on the basis of inferential signs, we say no; for they arise directly from the unmanifest (aviśeṣa).

Words, which have the moving and the unmoving as their basis, are the designators of the Supreme Self; because they enter into all things, they are primary [designators] of the Embodied One (the Self) in all bodies.
The self is understood from scripture not to be produced, and because it is eternal; and the eternity of the self is known from such scriptural passages as "He is eternal among the eternal."
It is certain that the Self is of the nature of knowledge and is eternal consciousness; seeing this, he rejoices, according to the Vedic revelation beginning with "He is a mass of knowledge."
On account of the scriptural statements regarding its departure, the description of its movement, and also the mention of its return, the self is said to be atomic in size.
Since the soul’s going and coming are accomplished by its own self, the doubt that the soul's atomicity is thereby established is not at all tenable here.

If it is argued that the self is not atomic because the scripture states "the self is great," we reply: that [greatness] refers to the Supreme Self; thus, it is certain that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic.
From the statement "the self is minute," the atom-like nature of the self follows; and from the name "the inferior one is the size of the tip of an awl," this is certain.
Even though the self is atomic, its experience of pleasure throughout the entire body is logical, just as the fragrance of sandalwood, though residing in only one spot, pervades the whole.

If it is argued that sandalwood becomes so [fragrant] due to a specific quality resulting from its particular state of being situated [on the body], we say no; for the Self, too, is said to abide within its own heart.
The Self, however, by pervading the body through its own quality of knowledge, experiences happiness; just as a gem and the like, by means of light alone, pervades everything and illuminates it.
If knowledge were to exist as something distinct from the knower merely by the cognition "I know," it would be like the fragrance of fragrant earth is distinct from the earth itself.
For, by the scriptural statement "the knower is indeed not the act of knowing," knowledge is spoken of here as distinct from the Self; therefore, knowledge must be separate from it.

Because it has the quality of knowledge as its essence, the Self may be designated as "knowledge"; furthermore, there is the designation "Brahman" based on the Vedic revelation: "Truth, Knowledge [is Brahman]."

And because it is a quality inherent in all selves, there is no fault in proclaiming one's knowledge; just as the designation "cow" arises from the connection with that specific nature of being a cow.
In this state [of deep sleep], there is the emergence of knowledge itself which was already present, just as masculinity and other traits present in childhood manifest in youth.
Even if the self were omnipresent and always possessed of knowledge, there would either be no perception at all, or else there would be a restriction to one or the other.
This self, however, is indeed the agent for those who perform sacrifices and meditations; this is so that the scriptures may be meaningful, whereas the qualities themselves possess no agency.

Because of the appropriation of the sense faculties and because of scriptural statements regarding his dwelling and so forth, this self is determined here to be the agent; thus, agency belongs to the self.
Based on such designations as "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," its agency in action is established; otherwise, it would have to be considered a third [category].

If the agency belongs to primordial nature (prakṛti) and not to the self (ātman), then just as there would be no fixed rule regarding perception, there would likewise be no fixed rule regarding the fruit [of action].

If that [prakṛti] alone were the agent, then the state of being the enjoyer would belong to prakṛti; however, because there is another who is the enjoyer, its [prakṛti's] status as the enjoyer is lost.

Since even meditative absorption (samādhi), which serves as the means to liberation, is impossible [for them], agency belongs to the self alone, as expressed in the passage beginning with "other than primordial nature" (prakṛter anya).
Even when tools such as an axe are present, the embodied soul acts with effort like a carpenter; thus, through the presence or absence of its own desire, it is both the agent and the non-agent.
The agency of the self must indeed be dependent upon the Supreme Self; for this Śruti declares accordingly: "He has entered within as the ruler."
For the sake of establishing both prohibition and injunction, He impels the individual soul by depending upon its own effort; thus, agency is indeed dependent on another.

The individual soul (jīva), however, is a part of Brahman, because of the designation of multiplicity; and also because of the designation of non-difference, as in the passage: "The Brahman is the masters."
From such mantras as "All beings are one foot of Him," it is certain that these very parts are indeed the Self of Brahman.
It is also stated in the Smṛti: "He is indeed a portion of myself in the world of living beings"; thus, his being a portion of Vāsudeva constitutes his status as having Brahman for his body.

Even though the individual soul (jīva) is a part of Brahman, its state as a living being does not truly exist in the Supreme; just as the nature of light and so forth does not belong to the gem and other such objects.
Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too is this power of the Supreme Brahman, according to the traditional teaching.

Even though individual souls are parts of Brahman, the possibility of both injunctions and prohibitions is appropriate due to the distinction of bodies, just as in the case of fire and other elements.
Furthermore, because they are distinct in each body and are atomic in nature, the non-confusion of pleasure and pain therein has been ascertained by the best of sages.

It is certain that all appearances would be causes; however, this is so only when one postulates the concealment (tirodhāna) and other states of the individual soul (jīva) despite the non-difference of Brahman.

The conceptualization of the Brahman-self and the individual self, which is rooted in the unseen principle (adṛṣṭa) and so forth, would certainly not be established because there is no fixed rule regarding those [unseen principles].

If it is argued that the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth arise from intention (abhisandhi), we say no; for in that case, no restrictive rule could possibly be stated regarding intention and the like.

If the individual soul (jīva) were the portion conditioned by ignorance (avidyā), there would be a restriction; for here, because of the inclusion of the limiting adjunct (upādhi), there is no movement of that which is unconditioned.
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Brahmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the second chapter.
The four senses arise from the Supreme Self like sparks from a fire; for that supreme Brāhmaṇa is indeed established as the vital breaths prior to creation.
Because it remains as Brahman alone even prior to creation, the scriptural statement "the seers are indeed the vital breaths" (prāṇā vā ṛṣayaḥ) is a figurative use of the plural.
And since the designation of things is preceded by their creation, it is certain that the senses are not denoted by the word "prāṇas."

One might suspect that "seven move" refers specifically to the seven cognitions, as indicated by the scriptural mention of their movement and the qualification "cognitions," which are the very same as the sense organs.
Since the vital breath (jīva) remains within the body through the assistance of speech, hands, and so forth, there are eleven sense organs; therefore, it is not the case that there are only seven.
For indeed, the senses are heard of in scripture as being minute through their functions such as apprehension; yet, for the purpose of meditation, they are said to be infinite.

For the vital breath arises as the most excellent from this [Self], just like space and the other elements; for there is a scriptural statement regarding its origin here: "From this, the vital breath is born."

Because of the statement regarding their separate origination, [the vital breath] is neither air nor its activity; it is established that the vital breath (prāṇa) is air that has attained some particular distinction.

Since it is merely a specific state of air, this [prāṇa] cannot be a separate element; for it is taught along with the sense organs in such passages as the "Dialogue of the Vital Breaths" (Prāṇasaṃvāda).

The defect attributed to the vital breath (prāṇa) on account of its being devoid of action does not apply at all, because the body and so forth are described as possessing actions such as maintenance and the like.
Just as the mind is designated by its different functions such as desire and so forth, so too the single vital breath is called prāṇa, apāna, and so on, according to its fivefold functions.

By the scriptural statement, "The vital breath does not depart," and so forth, the vital breath (prāṇa) must also be atomic; as for the greatness that was suspected [of it], that must refer to its pervasive power.
However, the presiding over the eyes and so forth by the Supreme Self through the volition of the individual soul (jīva) is understood from the scripture itself, such as the word "light" (jyotis).
Since the world of existing things is eternally presided over by another self, there must consequently be a presiding [deity] due to an unavoidable volition.
Even though all [the senses] possess the status of instruments, because they are designated as "senses" (indriya) with the exception of the Best One, that Best One does not become a sense.
Because its arising is taught as distinct from the sense-faculties together with the mind, and because the activity of the vital breath is specifically perceived even during deep sleep.
The creation of the world belongs only to the Supreme Self who has four faces; for it is He alone, performing the tripartition, who effects names, forms, and so forth.
But regarding the hearing, the mind, and the earth, it has been stated thus; for in passages such as "the food that is eaten," there is indeed no tripartition.
Among the elements that have been made tripartite, whichever one indeed possesses a predominance, that very thing is designated by the word expressive of it by the wise.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Brāhmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*.

Thus ends the second chapter of the *Brāhmasūtrārthapadyamālikā*, a work by the venerable Vaṇśaṭhakopa Vedāntadeśika Yatīndra Mahādeśika, who is adorned by forty-four consecrations as pontiff at the divine seat of the Śrīmad Ahobilamaṭha and who is richly endowed with the array of titles beginning with "Śrīmad Veda-mārga."
